newsitem.title: JORDAN: Jordan, British armies fight mock battles in desert.
newsitem.headline: Jordan, British armies fight mock battles in desert.

text.p: Jordanian and British infantry troops fought mock battles in the kingdom's desert on Wednesday at the end of 13 days of joint war games.

The explosions of mines, hand-grenades, mortar bombs, and anti-tank missiles echoed across the battlefield near Qatraneh, 90 km (57 miles) south of Amman as 500 fighters from both sides staged mock attacks under exercises codenamed "Desert King".
Jordanian and British army officers said the pre-planned exercises were not related to the latest military confrontation between Iraq and the United States.
Clouds of orange, green and blue smoke billowed in the sky as soldiers, clad in full camouflage combat attire, fired their guns to clear the ground for the offensives.
Later, a British-helicopter dropped ammunitition to support soldiers holding out in trenches in nearby hills.

Both armies have maintained strong cooperation despite King Hussein's dismissal in 1956 of British army commanders in Transjordan's Arab Legion -- then a focus of criticism from local and regional leaders -- to assert his own authority.
Army officers from both sides said they reaped benefits from the joint desert exercise, the second this year.
British and Jordanian battalions were able to compare the effectiveness of their weapons and war procedures.

Britain's Lieutenant-Colonel Clive Hodges, head of the Cyprus-based King's regiment, said his soldiers were able to fire all their weapons -- including Milan anti-tank missiles -- which is impossible on the divided island.
"We were practising our general war role and firing all the battalion's weapons live...as we are unable to fire those in Cyprus because we just have no space," he added.
"My regiment has very little experience operating in the desert which is a hostile environment and very different from the environment which we normally operate in."
Most of his men come from Manchester and Liverpool.
Acting Jordanian army chief Mohammad Salameh al-Hwayan said the exercises helped soldiers "gain professionalism and excellence".
The soldiers were expected to return to Cyprus by Monday.
